I should draft the root cause, executive summary, and assumptions carefully, making sure not to mischaracterize the Argus hold time as the outage duration while keeping the given 6-minute outage window (00:10–00:16) as stated. I need to flag clearly that the link between accelerator placement and the fraud-hold quality shift is correlational rather than proven, that the return to baseline after pinning supports but doesn't confirm causality, and that the error rate movement appears unrelated to baseline.

For the executive summary, I'll avoid naming specific components and instead describe the issue generally: the shop's fraud-check screening behaved differently for about 6 minutes, causing more orders to be held for review and more legitimate transactions flagged.

assumptions: Causality between the new accelerator and the shifted fraud-hold signal is inferred from timing (the device log line and the signal departure land in the same minute) and from recovery after pinning; the model's outputs on the two card types were not directly compared.
The recovery is attributed to the pin action, but the fault window had already closed at 00:16 and some of the improvement could be coincidental; no control was run.
The alternative explanation — fraud-scoring output quality degrading for an unrelated reason — was rated low confidence and never tested, so it is not ruled out.
Customer impact (orders held for review) is inferred from what the fraud-hold quality signal measures; no order-level or manual-review data was examined.
The ClientDisconnected errors in the logs are treated as pre-existing background noise unrelated to the incident, since they appear before onset and request-level metrics stayed at baseline.
The change log being empty for the 135 minutes before the alert is taken to mean no deploy or config change contributed; changes older than that window were not checked.
Why the replica was rescheduled onto a different card type (eviction, node turnover, scheduler choice) was not established.
input.executive_summary: Early on 8 October, the shop's automated fraud screening briefly started judging orders differently from normal, holding a higher share of them for review. The change began at 00:10 UTC and the behaviour was back to normal by 00:16 UTC, about six minutes later. Nothing was released or reconfigured; the cause was that one of the machines running the shop had been replaced with one using a different type of hardware accelerator, and the fraud-scoring model gave different answers on it. Checkout stayed up throughout — page speed, traffic and the share of failed requests were unchanged, so the practical effect was limited to some legitimate orders being flagged for manual review during those minutes. On-call automation detected the alert, identified the mismatched hardware, and restricted the shop's workloads to the hardware type the rest of the fleet uses, which restored normal scoring. A draft code change has been opened to prevent a recurrence.
input.root_cause: At 00:10:00Z a replacement replica of io-shop (io-shop-7d9c4f8b6-x2k9p) was scheduled onto an NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-40GB node while the other two serving replicas remained on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB cards; the fraud-scorer model produced materially different output on the A100, which pushed the fraud-hold quality series the paging rule watches off its baseline from exactly that minute. No deploy, rollout or feature-flag change landed in the window — the trigger was purely the heterogeneous accelerator placement, and pinning the service's pods back to the V100 card type returned the signal to baseline.
